content:
Mississippi is known for its blues heritage, Southern cuisine and historic towns. But travelers willing to venture off the beaten path will discover some of the state's most unexpected and memorable attractions.

A gas station serving a beloved local delicacy, a tiny museum hidden in an alley and a festival featuring hundreds of racing dachshunds are just a few reasons to take a detour. Here are five unexpected experiences worth adding to a Mississippi itinerary.

Oxford: A Gas Station Serving The Famous Chicken On A Stick

Not a restaurant, but a gas station in Oxford, home to the University of Mississippi, is one of the most popular late-night food destinations.

4 Corners Chevron, near the historic downtown Square, is famous for its chicken on a stick. It is an oversized, hand-battered and deep-fried boneless chicken tender served on a wooden skewer.

It has been a local favorite, particularly among Ole Miss students and football fans. After home games, visitors regularly line up outside the convenience store, sometimes well after midnight.

Unlike most restaurants, the gas station is open 24 hours a day. Hungry travelers can stop by any time.

Vicksburg: A Roadside Stand With A Cult-Favorite Sandwich

Travelers following Highway 61, the legendary Blues Highway, might mistake The Tomato Place for an ordinary roadside produce stand. However, hidden behind its colorful, somewhat overgrown exterior is a restaurant that has become a destination in its own right.

Owner Luke Hughes originally operated several fruit and vegetable stands. He started the restaurant only after a customer asked him to turn some of his tomatoes into a sandwich, then returned the following day for another.

Today, The Tomato Place at Vicksburg serves fried green tomato BLTs, po'boys, Southern lunches, fresh-squeezed lemonade and fruit smoothies in this Caribbean- and New Orleans-inspired diner with eclectic Americana decorations and souvenirs.

Hattiesburg: A Tiny Museum And A Giant Vintage Wonderland

More from this section

Hattiesburg Pocket Museum, opened in 2020, began as a tiny window display before expanding into an imaginative collection of miniature art installations in a neglected alley behind the town's historic Saenger Theater.

Visitors can discover rotating exhibits, murals, a miniature movie theater, a memorial bridge for departed pets and even a motion-activated disco.

According to the museum's organizers, more than 300,000 people have visited since its opening.

Five minutes from the Pocket Museum, travelers will find The Lucky Rabbit. It is a vintage marketplace spanning about 40,000 square feet across two historic buildings filled with antiques, collectibles, retro arcade games and elaborate displays inspired by nostalgic television shows and movies.

Starkville: Hundreds Of Dachshunds Race For Glory

Forget horse racing. In Starkville, one of the biggest annual spectacles features much shorter legs.

The Starkville Derby describes itself as the world's largest wiener dog race, bringing dachshunds and their owners to the city's Cotton District each spring. The 2026 event welcomed more than 315 competing dogs across 86 races. The next Derby is marked for May 1, 2027.

Visitors can extend their stay to explore the Cotton District's colorful architecture, restaurants and boutiques, or catch a Mississippi State University baseball game. The Bulldogs are scheduled to face Oklahoma at Dudy Noble Field on May 1, 2027, the same day as the Derby.

Coastal Mississippi: Explore Four Towns By Train

For a coastal adventure, travelers can leave their cars behind and board the Amtrak Mardi Gras Service, which connects New Orleans, Louisiana, with Mobile, Alabama, stopping in four Mississippi communities: Bay St. Louis, Gulfport, Biloxi, and Pascagoula. The journey takes approximately four hours, with two departures daily in each direction.

In Bay St. Louis, travelers can visit the 100 Men Hall, a historic African American music venue built in 1922 that once hosted legends such as Ray Charles, Etta James and James Brown.

In Gulfport, Fishbone Alley, a former utility alley is now a colorful gathering space filled with murals, public art, restaurants and bars.

Biloxi is home to the Ohr-O'Keefe Museum of Art, where architect Frank Gehry designed a striking collection of buildings celebrating the work of George E. Ohr, the eccentric ceramic artist nicknamed the "Mad Potter of Biloxi."

Pascagoula awaits visitors with a historical marker at Lighthouse Park commemorating a reported alien abduction. In October 1973, two local shipyard workers, Charles Hickson and Calvin Parker, claimed extraterrestrials took them aboard a spacecraft while they were fishing along the Pascagoula River. Their story attracted national attention and remains one of the town's most unusual claims to fame.
